# Two-Tower Retrieval Deep Dive -- Beyond InfoNCE (Google R1 Prep)

## Prerequisites

- InfoNCE / contrastive loss at the equation level
- Sampled softmax + popularity bias correction
- Dense vector retrieval and cosine / dot-product similarity
- Learning-to-rank metrics: NDCG, recall@K, MRR
- Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANN) at a high level

## Key Terms

- **Two-Tower** (Dual-Encoder Retrieval): Query and document encoded by independent towers; scoring is a pure dot product so doc embeddings can be precomputed and indexed offline
- **ANN** (Approximate Nearest Neighbor): Sublinear-time vector search over an offline index; trades exact recall for latency and memory
- **HNSW** (Hierarchical Navigable Small World): Graph-based ANN algorithm with high recall (95-97% @100) at sub-millisecond latency; memory-heavy but supports incremental insertion
- **IVF-PQ** (Inverted File + Product Quantization): Coarse clustering (IVF) followed by vector compression (PQ); low memory, needs periodic rebuild, recall typically 85-92% @100
- **InfoNCE** (Information Noise-Contrastive Estimation): Softmax cross-entropy over similarity scores across one positive and N negatives; the workhorse loss for two-tower training
- **TSS** (Training-Serving Skew): Any distribution or computation mismatch between what the model saw in training and what serves online; the single biggest source of offline-online metric divergence

## 0. Why Deep-Dive Past **InfoNCE** (Framing)

Staging-11 covers **InfoNCE** in isolation -- the loss, the temperature, the gradient. That is enough to pass an ML-fundamentals question but not a system-design question. Google R1 for L5/L6 ranking asks: 'you have a billion-doc corpus and a 10ms SLA; walk me through the retrieval stage.' The interesting answers are all architectural: the **Two-Tower** factorization itself, how you mine negatives without poisoning the model, which **ANN** index matches your update frequency, and why your offline recall@1000 can go up 3 points while online NDCG goes down.

This drill covers those four system-level concerns. The thread tying them together is **decoupling**: query and document are scored by a dot product with no cross-attention, which buys offline indexing but bans any feature that crosses the (q, d) boundary. Every tradeoff in the stack follows from that one constraint.

Oral shortcut: '**Two-tower** = dot product = offline index. Everything else -- negative mining, **HNSW** vs IVF, the offline/online gap -- is a second-order consequence of that first line.'

## 1. Why Two Towers -- Decoupled Scoring Buys the Index

The canonical architecture: a query tower maps (user features, context, text) to u in R^d, and an item tower maps (item features, text, metadata) to v in R^d. The score is a pure inner product:

Two-tower score: dot product of independently computed query and document embeddings:

$$s(q, d) = u_\theta(q)^\top v_\phi(d), \quad u, v \in \mathbb{R}^d$$

The critical property is that v_phi(d) depends only on d -- it never sees the query. That single constraint is what makes billion-scale retrieval possible. Concretely:

1. **Offline precomputation**: every doc embedding v is computed once per corpus snapshot, not once per query. On a 10^9-doc index with a 1B-param tower, that is the difference between a 10ms SLA and a 10-minute SLA.

2. **ANN index build**: once all v are fixed, a vector index (HNSW or **IVF-PQ**) is built over them. Online serving becomes encode(q) -> **ANN** search -- O(log N) or better instead of O(N).

3. **Fresh query features are free**: u_theta is recomputed every request, so real-time context (location, session, time of day) costs nothing extra. This is why two-tower dominates context-sensitive retrieval (DoorDash, YouTube home feed, Pinterest homefeed).

The cost is expressiveness. A cross-encoder can attend jointly over (q, d) tokens and learn 'query word A interacts with doc word B'; a two-tower cannot. Any feature that crosses the (q, d) boundary -- 'how many words in q appear in d', 'click-through rate of (q, d) pair' -- must live in the reranker, not the retriever. The standard production pattern is retrieval (two-tower) -> rerank (cross-encoder on top-K candidates):

Two-stage pipeline: cheap dot-product retrieval feeds expensive cross-attention rerank:

$$\text{retrieve}: \text{top-}K_{d} \; u^\top v \;\; \longrightarrow \;\; \text{rerank}: \mathrm{score}_{\text{cross}}(q, d)$$

System implications to mention in the oral answer:

- **Index refresh latency**: changing the item tower requires re-encoding the entire corpus -- plan for hours of rebuild time. Twin queries ('same item appears with different metadata') need versioning.

- **No late interaction**: models like ColBERT relax two-tower with per-token late interaction, paying ~10x the memory for a recall bump. Useful when you can afford it; Google's scale usually cannot.

- **User tower must be pure**: no feature that depends on the candidate document. Reviewers press on this -- if you say 'user embedding includes a signal of top candidates' you have violated the decoupling and lost the offline index.

Oral shortcut: 'Two towers means v has no knowledge of q, so v is precomputable, so an ANN index over v gives sub-millisecond retrieval. The architectural cost is no cross-attention, which is why we always add a reranker.'

## 2. Negative Sampling -- Four Strategies, Four Failure Modes

Two-tower training with **InfoNCE** is pure softmax over a small set of negatives; model quality is dominated by the negative distribution. The full corpus softmax is infeasible, so every production system picks from four strategies (usually mixed).

InfoNCE over K negatives: the choice of the K-negative distribution is the dominant design variable:

$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{\exp(u^\top v^+ / \tau)}{\exp(u^\top v^+ / \tau) + \sum_{j=1}^{K} \exp(u^\top v_j^- / \tau)}$$

**(a) Random negatives**: draw K items uniformly from the corpus. Cheap, unbiased relative to the corpus prior. *Failure mode*: most random items are trivially negative -- 'query = pizza' vs 'doc = power drill' is not a hard problem. The model learns the coarse topic but never the within-topic fine distinctions that actually drive user satisfaction.

**(b) In-batch negatives**: use the other items' positives in the same minibatch as negatives for this row. K = batch_size - 1 for free, no extra forward passes. *Failure mode*: **popularity bias** -- frequent items appear as positives AND as negatives proportionally to their frequency. The gradient over-penalizes popular items, collapsing them away from frequent queries. The textbook correction is the sampled-softmax **logit correction**:

Popularity-corrected logit: subtract the log sampling probability to recover unbiased softmax over the full corpus (Bengio-Senecal 2008, YouTube DNN):

$$s'(q, d_j) = u^\top v_j - \log p_j, \quad p_j = P(\text{item } j \text{ sampled})$$

Without the correction, in-batch negatives bias the index against the head of the distribution -- exactly the items the reranker most relies on.

**(c) Hard negatives**: at training step t, run ANN search with the current model and take the top-K items that were NOT clicked as negatives for step t+1. Sharpens the decision boundary around the margin that matters. *Failure mode 1*: **false negatives** -- the user did not click not because the item is irrelevant but because they did not see it (below the fold, next page). Training pushes relevant items away from the query. *Failure mode 2*: **self-reinforcing loop** -- hard negatives from the current model encode the current model's biases; training on them tightens those biases instead of correcting them. Standard mitigation: mine from a **snapshot** of the previous version, not the live model.

**(d) Mixed / curriculum**: the production default -- a blend such as 50% in-batch, 30% random, 20% hard. The ratios are a hyperparameter that deserves sweeping. *Failure mode*: the blend is often chosen once and never re-tuned when the corpus or query distribution shifts.

Cross-cutting pitfall: **positive-only bias**. Training pairs come from clicks; clicks happen only on impressed items. Items that pi0 never surfaced are never positives AND never hard negatives -- they are invisible. This is the same selection-bias problem that **IPS** (see IPS drill, T-P0-418) addresses for evaluation, and it matters for retrieval training too: you cannot learn to retrieve what you never logged.

Oral shortcut: 'Random is unbiased but too easy; in-batch is cheap but popularity-biased (subtract log p_j); hard is sharp but has false negatives and a self-reinforcing loop (mine from a snapshot). Mix all three. Selection bias on positives is the problem that mixing cannot fix.'

## 3. HNSW vs IVF-PQ -- Recall, Latency, Memory, Updates

The two dominant production ANN indexes have orthogonal failure modes; picking the right one is a system-design decision, not a tuning one. Summary sheet:

**HNSW vs IVF-PQ vs Flat -- Production ANN Tradeoffs**

|  | HNSW | IVF-PQ | Flat (exact) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure | Multi-layer proximity graph | IVF cells + PQ-compressed vectors | Linear scan |
| Build time | Slow (minutes-hours at 1e8) | Medium (IVF k-means + PQ train) | None |
| Query latency | Sub-millisecond (~0.3-0.5ms) | ~1ms (nprobe dependent) | O(N) -- seconds at 1e6+ |
| Memory | High (~2-4x vector size for graph) | Low (4-16 bytes per vector after PQ) | Exact -- 4 bytes * d per vector |
| Recall@100 | 95-98% | 85-92% (PQ-loss dependent) | 100% (ground truth) |
| Incremental insert | Supported natively | Requires IVF reassignment, usually rebuild | Free |
| Distance metric | Dot / cosine / L2 (all work) | L2 native; dot via transform | Any |
| Failure mode | Memory blowup past ~1e8 vectors | Recall collapse on heavy-tail queries | Latency kills it past ~1e6 |


## 3.1 When to Pick Which

**Pick HNSW when**: corpus fits in memory (roughly under 10^8 vectors at d=128), latency SLA is tight (under 1ms), and items update incrementally (store-open / store-close, product availability flips). Typical fit: DoorDash merchant retrieval, Pinterest pin retrieval for a given board.

**Pick IVF-PQ when**: corpus is 10^9+ vectors and memory is the binding constraint, updates are batch (daily or weekly rebuild is acceptable), and you can tolerate 90-92% recall with a rerank stage to compensate. Typical fit: YouTube video corpus, Google Web index retrieval cells.

**Pick Flat when**: you are debugging, building the ground truth for recall measurement, or your corpus is under 10^5 and latency does not matter. Never ship Flat to prod at scale.

**Hybrid**: many systems use IVF-PQ at the outer layer (coarse cell routing) and HNSW within each cell (fine search inside the retrieved cells). Faiss composite indexes do this out of the box.

## 3.2 Recall vs Latency Curve

Both indexes expose a recall/latency knob -- 'ef_search' for HNSW, 'nprobe' for IVF-PQ. Interviewers press on how you tune it:

- Set the recall target at the retrieval stage to be comfortably higher than you need downstream -- e.g., if the reranker sees top-100 and you want 95% effective recall, tune the ANN for 97-98% recall@1000 so the rerank has headroom.

- Always over-retrieve: request top-(K * 2-5) from ANN and let the reranker prune. The marginal latency cost is flat; the recall lift is large because ANN's 2-5% miss rate is uncorrelated with rerank error.

- Report recall as **recall-vs-ground-truth-Flat**, not 'recall@K' against training labels -- you want to separate index approximation error from model quality error.

Oral shortcut: 'HNSW for in-memory sub-ms, IVF-PQ for billion-scale with batch updates. Over-retrieve by 2-5x and let the reranker clean up. Tune ef_search / nprobe against ground-truth Flat, not against training labels.'

## 4. Offline Recall@K vs Online NDCG -- The Skew That Matters

The failure mode a Google R1 interviewer is looking for: 'we shipped v2, offline recall@1000 improved by 3 points, online NDCG dropped by 0.5 points, traffic moved to baseline.' This is not a measurement error; it is **training-serving skew** (**TSS**) with five concrete sources. Naming all five is the senior-level answer.

**Source 1: ANN approximation skew.** Offline recall is typically evaluated against Flat (exact) top-K; online serving uses HNSW or IVF-PQ with a 3-10% miss rate. The offline number does not reflect what users actually see. *Detection*: measure 'index recall' = recall(ANN top-K, Flat top-K) as a standalone metric; trust no recall number that does not separate model recall from index recall.

**Source 2: Feature skew.** The query tower uses features (session history, location, real-time context) that are computed differently offline (from logs, deduplicated, backfilled) vs online (streaming, fresh, with clock-skew). *Detection*: re-score a held-out logged query with BOTH the offline pipeline and the online pipeline; compare the two score distributions. Any KL divergence above ~0.05 is a smoking gun.

**Source 3: Reward misalignment.** Offline recall counts 'relevant' = 'user clicked'; online NDCG uses graded labels or a different reward model. A retriever trained to maximize click-positive recall may retrieve clickbait over satisfaction-positive items -- online NDCG falls while recall@1000 rises. *Detection*: evaluate offline recall with the SAME relevance function the online metric uses, not with 'is clicked'.

**Source 4: Rerank inversion.** Retrieval ranks by dot product; the production list is reranked by a cross-encoder. A retriever that brings candidates in a different order can still expose the same set, but the reranker's calibration was trained on the old retriever's score distribution -- when that shifts, ranker calibration breaks (see T-P0-417 Calibration drill for why). *Detection*: re-train or temperature-recalibrate the reranker after every retriever swap; offline-eval the FULL pipeline (retrieve + rerank), not just retrieval.

**Source 5: Popularity distribution drift.** Offline training negatives are sampled from the historical corpus distribution; online, the active candidate set skews toward fresher, more popular items. If in-batch logit correction used the wrong p_j distribution, head items will be over-suppressed online. *Detection*: monitor the head/tail recall breakdown. If head recall dropped and tail recall rose, popularity correction is over-fired.

The canonical full-stack unbiased-evaluation approach:

Debiased offline NDCG via IPS (see T-P0-418 drill): divides out selection and position bias so offline and online are comparable:

$$\widehat{\mathrm{NDCG}}(\pi_{\text{new}}) = \sum_{q, d \in \text{logs}} \frac{c_{q,d}}{p_{k_0(q,d)}} \cdot g_\pi(q,d)$$

Oral shortcut: 'Five skews: index recall vs Flat, feature freshness, reward function, rerank calibration, popularity drift. Isolate each with a targeted offline diagnostic before shipping. Offline recall@K alone is not a ship gate; debiased offline NDCG is closer, and a small A/B is still required.'

## 5. Numerical Sanity Check -- Putting Scales on It

Concrete numbers interviewers like to hear:

- Typical embedding dim d: 64-256. Higher d beyond ~256 rarely helps recall but hurts ANN latency linearly.

- HNSW memory: ~(4d + 8M) bytes per vector, where M is the graph degree (typical M=16). At d=128, M=16: ~640 bytes per vector. 10^8 vectors -> 64 GB RAM. That is where HNSW tops out on a single host.

- IVF-PQ memory after PQ compression: 8-16 bytes per vector. 10^9 vectors -> 8-16 GB. That is why IVF-PQ is the only choice at web scale.

- In-batch negatives at batch size 8192: K=8191 negatives for free per positive. This is why two-tower training scales more easily to massive batches -- you get effective K growth with no extra forward passes on the item tower.

- Temperature tau: 0.05 to 0.1 is typical. Too small (<0.01) -> gradient concentrates on the nearest negative, training becomes unstable. Too large (>0.5) -> loss is nearly uniform and the model learns slowly.

- Rebuild cadence: HNSW can accept writes in seconds; IVF-PQ typically rebuilds daily. If the task requires fresh-within-minutes, HNSW or a tiered index is mandatory.

### 2-Minute Oral Self-Check

- [ ] Two-tower architecture: independent u_theta(q), v_phi(d), score = u . v
- [ ] Decoupling enables offline precomputation + ANN index (this is the whole win)
- [ ] Cost: no cross-attention -> cross-features must live in the reranker
- [ ] Negative sampling: (a) random, (b) in-batch (correct with -log p_j), (c) hard (mine from snapshot), (d) mixed
- [ ] In-batch popularity bias fixed by sampled-softmax log correction
- [ ] Hard-negative failure modes: false negatives + self-reinforcing loop
- [ ] HNSW: graph, sub-ms, incremental, memory-heavy, picks at <=1e8 scale
- [ ] IVF-PQ: coarse + PQ compression, memory-light, batch rebuild, picks at 1e9+ scale
- [ ] Over-retrieve by 2-5x into the reranker; tune ef_search / nprobe against Flat
- [ ] Five **TSS** sources: index recall, feature skew, reward function, rerank calibration, popularity drift
- [ ] Offline recall@K alone is not a ship gate; use debiased NDCG + small A/B
